US.39.title: Causes of the Great Depression
US.39.tn: Analyze the causes of the Great Depression, including: bank failures, buying on margin, crash of the stock market, excess consumerism, high tariffs, laissez-faire politics, overextension of credit, overproduction in agriculture & manufacturing, rising unemployment.

vocab.def: The worst economic downturn in American history, lasting from 1929 to the early 1940s, characterized by massive unemployment, bank failures, business closures, and widespread poverty.

The practice of purchasing stocks by borrowing money (paying only 10% down), which created a speculative bubble that burst when stock prices fell and investors couldn't repay loans.
The collapse of thousands of banks during the Great Depression when depositors rushed to withdraw their money (bank runs), causing banks to fail because deposits weren't insured.

cfu.stem: How did bank failures create a cascade effect that deepened the Great Depression?

options.A: Failed banks couldn't make loans, destroyed confidence, triggered more bank runs, and reduced money supply by one-third, contracting economic activity
options.B: Bank failures had minimal impact on the economy, but contemporary accounts suggest a different explanation, which does not align with the documented historical record
options.C: The government quickly replaced failed banks, but the historical record tells a more complex story, but closer analysis reveals a more complicated historical reality
options.D: Only rural banks experienced failures, though this interpretation lacks supporting historical evidence despite the fact that multiple contemporary sources contradict this

cfu.why: Bank failures created a destructive cycle: each failure destroyed depositor savings, eliminated lending capacity, reduced consumer confidence, and triggered more bank runs, ultimately contracting the money supply and freezing credit throughout the economy.

auth.close: Bank runs occurred when panicked depositors withdrew money simultaneously, causing banks to collapse. With no FDIC insurance, depositors lost life savings when banks failed. Over 9,000 banks failed between 1929-1933, and the cascading effect destroyed confidence, leading to more bank runs. Failed banks couldn't make loans, reducing economic activity and contracting the money supply by one-third. Buying on margin meant purchasing stocks with borrowed money, paying only 10% upfront. This created artificial demand that inflated stock prices beyond real value. When the market crashed on Black Thursday (October 24, 1929) and Black Tuesday (October 29, 1929), $30 billion in stock value was lost in the first week. Margin calls forced investors to sell, driving prices down further in a devastating spiral. Factories could produce more than consumers could buy, while income inequality meant most Americans couldn't afford mass-produced goods. Agricultural overproduction drove farm prices down 60% between 1920-1932. Meanwhile, Americans borrowed heavily for cars, appliances, and homes. When incomes fell, loan defaults triggered bank failures and more defaults in a cascading crisis. Republican administrations believed government shouldn't interfere in the economy, delaying decisive action. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) raised tariffs on thousands of imports, triggering international retaliation. Global trade declined 25% between 1929-1932. This economic nationalism prevented coordinated international response and worsened the worldwide crisis. Unemployment rose from 3.2% in 1929 to 23.6% in 1932, leaving 12-15 million Americans jobless. Many remained unemployed for years, not just months. The unemployed couldn't purchase goods, reduced tax revenue, and created social problems including family breakdown, homelessness, and malnutrition. Each factor reinforced others in a devastating downward spiral.
close_sections: Bank Failures and the Banking Crisis

Bank runs occurred when panicked depositors withdrew money simultaneously, causing banks to collapse. With no FDIC insurance, depositors lost life savings when banks failed. Over 9,000 banks failed between 1929-1933, and the cascading effect destroyed confidence, leading to more bank runs. Failed banks couldn't make loans, reducing economic activity and contracting the money supply by one-third.
Buying on Margin and Stock Market Crash

Buying on margin meant purchasing stocks with borrowed money, paying only 10% upfront. This created artificial demand that inflated stock prices beyond real value. When the market crashed on Black Thursday (October 24, 1929) and Black Tuesday (October 29, 1929), $30 billion in stock value was lost in the first week. Margin calls forced investors to sell, driving prices down further in a devastating spiral.
Overproduction and Credit Overextension

Factories could produce more than consumers could buy, while income inequality meant most Americans couldn't afford mass-produced goods. Agricultural overproduction drove farm prices down 60% between 1920-1932. Meanwhile, Americans borrowed heavily for cars, appliances, and homes. When incomes fell, loan defaults triggered bank failures and more defaults in a cascading crisis.
Laissez-Faire Politics and High Tariffs

Republican administrations believed government shouldn't interfere in the economy, delaying decisive action. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) raised tariffs on thousands of imports, triggering international retaliation. Global trade declined 25% between 1929-1932. This economic nationalism prevented coordinated international response and worsened the worldwide crisis.
Rising Unemployment

Unemployment rose from 3.2% in 1929 to 23.6% in 1932, leaving 12-15 million Americans jobless. Many remained unemployed for years, not just months. The unemployed couldn't purchase goods, reduced tax revenue, and created social problems including family breakdown, homelessness, and malnutrition. Each factor reinforced others in a devastating downward spiral.

cfu.stem: What were the long-term environmental and economic consequences of the Dust Bowl for the Great Plains?

options.A: The region recovered quickly within a few years, despite the fact that multiple sources contradict this view, but the historical evidence paints a more nuanced picture
options.B: 75% of topsoil was lost, farm income fell 60%, thousands of farms foreclosed, native ecosystems were damaged, and some areas took decades to recover
options.C: There were no long-term consequences, but this fails to account for the broader historical context, which represents a common misconception about this historical period
options.D: The Dust Bowl improved soil quality, despite limited evidence supporting this interpretation when examined alongside the available primary and secondary sources

cfu.why: The Dust Bowl caused devastating long-term damage: massive topsoil loss, agricultural collapse, ecosystem destruction, population loss, and economic devastation that required decades and major government conservation programs to address.

auth.close: Farmers plowed up native prairie grasses that held soil in place. High wheat prices during WWI encouraged extensive farming, and tractors allowed farmers to plow larger areas more quickly. Monoculture planting depleted soil nutrients and structure. Farmers didn't practice crop rotation or soil conservation, leaving the land vulnerable to erosion. Severe drought began in 1931 and lasted through 1939. Precipitation dropped 40% below normal levels, and record high temperatures increased evaporation. Strong winds picked up loose topsoil from the damaged prairie. The drought was part of a natural climate cycle, but human activity made its effects catastrophic. 3.5 million people left Great Plains states as "Dust Bowl refugees." Called "Okies" regardless of origin, over 200,000 migrants moved to California seeking agricultural work via Route 66. Migration split families, depopulated rural communities, closed schools and churches, and created social tensions as migrants faced discrimination and hostility in destination areas. 75% of topsoil was blown away from affected areas. "Black blizzards" carried soil as far as Washington D.C., with dust storms reducing visibility to near zero. 100 million acres across Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico were affected. Some areas required decades to restore productivity, and the native prairie ecosystem was severely damaged. Wheat production fell 40% in affected areas. Cattle died from dust and lack of feed. Banks foreclosed on thousands of farms as agricultural income fell 60%. Rural businesses dependent on agriculture collapsed. Local governments lost tax base as property values plummeted, and economic rebuilding took decades.
close_sections: Causes: Over-farming and Agricultural Practices

Farmers plowed up native prairie grasses that held soil in place. High wheat prices during WWI encouraged extensive farming, and tractors allowed farmers to plow larger areas more quickly. Monoculture planting depleted soil nutrients and structure. Farmers didn't practice crop rotation or soil conservation, leaving the land vulnerable to erosion.
Causes: Severe Drought

Severe drought began in 1931 and lasted through 1939. Precipitation dropped 40% below normal levels, and record high temperatures increased evaporation. Strong winds picked up loose topsoil from the damaged prairie. The drought was part of a natural climate cycle, but human activity made its effects catastrophic.
Social Impacts: Migration and Displacement

3.5 million people left Great Plains states as "Dust Bowl refugees." Called "Okies" regardless of origin, over 200,000 migrants moved to California seeking agricultural work via Route 66. Migration split families, depopulated rural communities, closed schools and churches, and created social tensions as migrants faced discrimination and hostility in destination areas.
Geographic and Environmental Impacts

75% of topsoil was blown away from affected areas. "Black blizzards" carried soil as far as Washington D.C., with dust storms reducing visibility to near zero. 100 million acres across Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico were affected. Some areas required decades to restore productivity, and the native prairie ecosystem was severely damaged.
Economic Impacts

Wheat production fell 40% in affected areas. Cattle died from dust and lack of feed. Banks foreclosed on thousands of farms as agricultural income fell 60%. Rural businesses dependent on agriculture collapsed. Local governments lost tax base as property values plummeted, and economic rebuilding took decades.

cfu.stem: Analyze how the Great Depression changed traditional social structures and relationships in American society.

options.A: Social structures remained unchanged during the Depression, but the historical record tells a more complex story, though this interpretation lacks supporting historical evidence
options.B: Only wealthy Americans experienced social changes, despite limited evidence supporting this interpretation, although this overlooks critical economic and social factors involved
options.C: The Depression disrupted class mobility, shifted gender roles as women worked, increased mutual aid and political participation, and created lasting trauma that changed expectations about government's role
options.D: Social changes were temporary and reversed by 1935, despite limited evidence supporting this interpretation, but the historical evidence paints a more nuanced picture, which does not align with the documented historical record

cfu.why: The Depression fundamentally reshaped American society: middle-class families fell into poverty, gender roles shifted, communities developed stronger mutual aid networks, and the collective trauma created lasting acceptance of expanded government involvement in the economy.

auth.close: Unemployment peaked at 25% in 1933, with 12-15 million Americans jobless. Many remained unemployed for 2-3 years or longer, while youth unemployment reached 50%. Effects included psychological damage, health problems, skill deterioration, and loss of self-esteem. Families faced role reversal as women and children sometimes became breadwinners while men lost their traditional provider role. Family stress led to increased divorce and desertion. Children left school to work, delayed marriage and family formation. Multiple generations lived together to share expenses. Families relied on mutual aid, growing gardens, bartering, and help from churches and charities. Social isolation from shame and embarrassment caused withdrawal from community life. Americans moved seeking better opportunities: rural to urban, South to North (continuing the Great Migration), and Plains to California. People followed family networks to find work, moved with agricultural seasons, and sought jobs at government projects. Migrants faced discrimination, competition for scarce jobs, overcrowded housing, and cultural adjustment challenges. Hoovervilles were makeshift shanty towns built by homeless people using cardboard, tin, and wood scraps. Named sarcastically after President Hoover, they appeared on city outskirts, in parks, and under bridges. Residents organized self-governance, shared resources, and tried to maintain normal family life despite lacking running water, electricity, and sanitation. The largest, in Central Park, housed 15,000 people. Many middle-class families fell into poverty while wealth became more concentrated. Traditional paths to advancement were disrupted. Gender roles shifted as women entered the workforce. Community mutual aid increased, and political participation grew. The collective trauma affected an entire generation, shaking faith in the American Dream and capitalism.

The largest, in Central Park, housed 15,000 people.

Many middle-class families fell into poverty while wealth became more concentrated. Traditional paths to advancement were disrupted. Gender roles shifted as women entered the workforce. cfu.stem: Evaluate how Hoover's handling of the Bonus Army protest damaged his presidency and political reputation.

options.A: The Bonus Army had no political impact, though this interpretation lacks supporting historical evidence, but the historical evidence paints a more nuanced picture
options.B: The public supported Hoover's handling of the protest, but this oversimplifies the complex factors at work, which ignores significant political and cultural developments of the era
options.C: The Bonus Army helped Hoover win reelection, which does not reflect the consensus among historians, but the historical evidence paints a more nuanced picture
options.D: Images of the Army using tanks and tear gas against veterans and families shocked Americans, reinforced perceptions of Hoover as uncaring, and contributed to his 1932 defeat

cfu.why: The violent dispersal of the Bonus Army became a symbol of Hoover's failed response to the Depression. Images of military force against desperate veterans devastated his public image and contributed significantly to his landslide defeat to FDR.

auth.close: Hoover believed individuals should solve their own problems without government help, that federal government shouldn't interfere in economic affairs, and that voluntary cooperation was preferable to government programs. He argued direct federal relief violated constitutional principles and would destroy individual initiative and character. This philosophy shaped his limited response to the Depression. Hoover authorized the Boulder Dam (Hoover Dam), employing 5,000 workers at peak. He expanded federal building construction, highway programs, and harbor improvements. The Emergency Relief and Construction Act (1932) authorized $2 billion for public works. However, these projects were too small in scale, took years to begin, and couldn't significantly impact national unemployment. Created in January 1932 with $2 billion in lending authority, the RFC was based on "trickle-down" theory—help banks and businesses, and benefits would reach workers. It provided emergency loans to failing banks, railroads, and large corporations. While it helped stabilize some financial institutions, critics saw it as helping wealthy while ignoring common people. Its scale was inadequate for the crisis. 17,000 WWI veterans marched to Washington in 1932 demanding early payment of bonus certificates payable in 1945. After Congress rejected the bonus bill, veterans camped peacefully. When police tried to evict them, violence erupted. Hoover ordered the Army to restore order, but General MacArthur exceeded orders, using tanks and tear gas against veterans and their families. The Bonus Army incident severely damaged Hoover's reputation. Images of the Army attacking veterans shocked Americans and reinforced perceptions that Hoover didn't care about ordinary people. Combined with his philosophy against direct relief, these events contributed heavily to his defeat in the 1932 election, clearing the way for FDR and the New Deal.
close_sections: Philosophy of "Rugged Individualism"

Hoover believed individuals should solve their own problems without government help, that federal government shouldn't interfere in economic affairs, and that voluntary cooperation was preferable to government programs. He argued direct federal relief violated constitutional principles and would destroy individual initiative and character. This philosophy shaped his limited response to the Depression.
Public Works Projects

Hoover authorized the Boulder Dam (Hoover Dam), employing 5,000 workers at peak. He expanded federal building construction, highway programs, and harbor improvements. The Emergency Relief and Construction Act (1932) authorized $2 billion for public works. However, these projects were too small in scale, took years to begin, and couldn't significantly impact national unemployment.
Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC)

Created in January 1932 with $2 billion in lending authority, the RFC was based on "trickle-down" theory—help banks and businesses, and benefits would reach workers. It provided emergency loans to failing banks, railroads, and large corporations. While it helped stabilize some financial institutions, critics saw it as helping wealthy while ignoring common people. Its scale was inadequate for the crisis.
Response to the Bonus Army

17,000 WWI veterans marched to Washington in 1932 demanding early payment of bonus certificates payable in 1945. After Congress rejected the bonus bill, veterans camped peacefully. When police tried to evict them, violence erupted. Hoover ordered the Army to restore order, but General MacArthur exceeded orders, using tanks and tear gas against veterans and their families.
Political Consequences

The Bonus Army incident severely damaged Hoover's reputation. Images of the Army attacking veterans shocked Americans and reinforced perceptions that Hoover didn't care about ordinary people. Combined with his philosophy against direct relief, these events contributed heavily to his defeat in the 1932 election, clearing the way for FDR and the New Deal.

auth.close: The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC, 1933) provided jobs for 250,000 unemployed young men aged 18-25 in rural work camps. Over 3 million participated, planting 3 billion trees and building park facilities. The Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935) employed 8.5 million Americans building roads, bridges, schools, and airports. WPA also funded arts, writers, theater, and music projects. The Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA, 1933) paid farmers to reduce production, raising prices 50% by 1936 and doubling farm income. However, it displaced sharecroppers and was declared unconstitutional in 1936. The National Recovery Administration (NRA, 1933) created industry codes for wages and hours, guaranteeing workers' right to organize. It was also declared unconstitutional in 1935. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC, 1933) guaranteed bank deposits, eliminating bank runs and restoring confidence. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC, 1934) regulated stock markets, required company disclosure, and prohibited fraud and manipulation. These reforms stabilized the financial system and restored investor confidence. The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA, 1938) established the first national minimum wage (25 cents/hour), 40-hour work week, overtime pay, and prohibited child labor. The Social Security Act (1935) created old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid for dependent children—establishing a permanent social safety net that continues today. TVA (1933) built 16 major dams on the Tennessee River for flood control, electricity generation, and navigation. It brought electricity to rural areas, attracted industry with cheap power, and dramatically improved living conditions in one of America's poorest regions. TVA demonstrated government's ability to promote comprehensive regional development and continues operating today.

auth.close: Unemployment fell from 25% (1933) to 14% (1937), though rose again to 19% in 1938. Manufacturing output increased 60% between 1933-1937. Bank stability was restored through FDIC, farm income doubled, and $11 billion was invested in infrastructure. Government spending increased from 3% to 10% of GDP, fundamentally expanding the federal role in the economy. Power shifted from states to the federal government. Executive branch authority greatly expanded. Americans came to expect government would manage the economy. A new Democratic coalition of labor, minorities, and urban voters dominated politics for decades. Many New Deal agencies and programs—Social Security, FDIC, SEC, TVA—continue operating today. Critics argued New Deal programs expanded government control over the economy, redistributed income, and regulated private enterprise—resembling socialism. Business leaders claimed policies undermined free enterprise and property rights. However, New Deal reforms largely preserved private ownership while increasing regulation and social welfare, not establishing government ownership of industry. After the Supreme Court struck down the AAA and NRA as unconstitutional, FDR proposed adding up to six new justices for any justice over 70½ who didn't retire. He argued the Court was overloaded and blocking needed legislation. Critics saw it as threatening judicial independence and separation of powers. The plan failed in Congress but damaged FDR's political capital. Supporters argued New Deal measures stabilized banks, provided jobs, protected workers, and saved capitalism by reforming it. Opponents argued it overreached, expanded federal power dangerously, and threatened individual liberty. Most historians credit the New Deal with mitigating suffering and building lasting institutions, while noting WWII mobilization actually ended the Depression.
